title: Encoding Matters: A Qubit-Efficient Reformulation for Quantum Resilient Routing
authors: Emanuele G. Dalla Torre, Bat-El Friedman, Daniel Porat
abstract: Qubits are powerful computational resources because each additional qubit doubles the size of the accessible state space. This expressive power comes at a cost: adding qubits also increases circuit size, constraint overhead, and exposure to hardware noise. These limitations are especially critical for near-term quantum computers, making the number of qubits required to formulate a problem a central practical concern. In this work, we present a method for efficiently mapping logistics and routing problems onto qubits through structure-aware encoding reduction. We demonstrate the method on a benchmark problem of latency-resilient routing under dual-link failures. For this benchmark, the reduced formulation substantially lowers both the qubit count and the compiled circuit complexity while preserving the original optimization task. By running the reduced model on the same trapped-ion quantum computer as the benchmark, we obtain a 100X improvement in the success probability. This finding shows how careful problem formulation can make current quantum hardware substantially more effective for practical optimization.
summary: This work introduces a structure-aware encoding reduction technique to efficiently map complex routing problems onto quantum circuits, significantly reducing the required number of qubits and circuit complexity. By applying this reduction to a benchmark routing problem, the authors achieved a 100X improvement in success probability when running the model on a trapped-ion quantum computer. This demonstrates that careful problem formulation can make current quantum hardware much more effective for practical optimization tasks.
main_problem: The paper addresses the critical resource overhead (qubit count and circuit size) when mapping complex logistics and routing problems onto quantum circuits for near-term quantum computers.
main_result: A structure-aware encoding reduction method was developed that substantially lowers the required qubit count (from 24 to 7 for a benchmark) and improved the success probability on a trapped-ion QPU by 100X.
method: The core method involves applying deterministic, local logical rules to simplify the standard canonical QUBO encoding of graph problems, thereby reducing the number of necessary variables without altering the optimization objective.
model_or_system: The problem is formulated as a QUBO model derived from graph optimization problems (like latency-resilient routing). Benchmarking was performed on a trapped-ion quantum computer, and the optimization was executed using QAOA circuits.
key_observables: Qubit count (reduction from 24 to 7), compiled circuit complexity (gates), and hardware success probability (100X improvement).
important_parameters: The penalty coefficient $\alpha=10$ was used to enforce constraints in the QUBO formulation.
main_assumptions: The reduction rules are assumed to be local and deterministic, and the method's generalizability is claimed for other network and logistic problems.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the workflow showing the reduction from the original formulation to the reduced model. Figure 2 details the application of the five reduction rules to the benchmark case. Figure 3 compares the resource metrics (qubits, gates) between the canonical and reduced encodings.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of resource overhead in quantum encoding, details the structure-aware reduction method using five specific rules, validates the reduction via exhaustive enumeration, and finally benchmarks the reduced model on a trapped-ion QPU, comparing results against the canonical encoding.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computation, the explicit benchmarking on trapped-ion hardware provides direct experimental validation of encoding efficiency, which is crucial for understanding the practical limits of quantum simulation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Workflow for the proposed approach to solving net- work optimization problems. The highlighted step (3) repre- sents the rule-based encoding reduction that transforms the 24-qubit canonical formulation into a 7-qubit representation, before simulation and hardware execution.

FIG. 2: Rule-based reduction of the canonical encoding for the S2 benchmark case executed on quantum hardware, with paths to (a) T1 and (b) T2. Each annotation of the form “#N →q” denotes the application of the Nth reduction rule, map- ping a canonical variable either to a fixed value or to one of the surviving logical variables. The final reduced encoding contains the seven logical variables q0, . . . , q6 and their com- plementaries ¯qi = 1 −qi.

FIG. 3: Comparison between the canonical benchmark en- coding (gray) and the proposed reduced encoding (orange). The four groups report the number of qubits, the number of two-qubit entangling gates, the ideal ground-state success probability, and the hardware optimal-solution probability, respectively.
